results.ask: What's special about my block? I'm on 46th Ave between Moraga and Noriega.
results.expect: calls about_block; gives the block's own figures and something pinned nearby, with sources; cites
results.answer:
A few things stand out on 46th Ave between Moraga and Noriega:

- Your block sits about 39 feet above sea level, 0.2 miles from Ocean Beach, and most homes went up around 1941 — the tail end of the big Sunset building boom, just before wartime rules halted construction (SF Assessor's 2023 roll; USGS).
- Two blocks east, at 43rd and Moraga, Henry Doelger's Freedom House opened in 1942 — one of his last model homes before the war stopped building (Western Neighborhoods Project; SF Planning's Sunset builders context statement).
- A quarter mile west, the Noriega seawall dates from the 1980s, and Public Works moves tens of thousands of cubic yards of drifted sand there most years — timed for after the plovers leave (SPUR; SF Public Works, June 2023).
- The archive has old photographs pinned near your block: two at 46th & Moraga ([wnp58.929](https://opensfhistory.org/Display/wnp58.929.jpg), [wnp58.923](https://opensfhistory.org/Display/wnp58.923.jpg)) and three at 45th & Noriega, from OpenSFHistory.

Street cleaning: east side Mondays 1st & 3rd, noon–2pm (next Nov 16); west side Thursdays 1st/3rd/5th, noon–2pm (next Nov 19), per the city's sweeping schedule. The signs on the block are the last word.

If you know something about the block — who built your house, what the corner used to be — I'd be glad to add it to the notes for the next person who asks.

results.expect: uses the block the neighbor shared without asking for cross streets; cites
results.answer:
A few things, starting closest:

- Your block sits about 39 feet above the sea, and most homes went up around 1941 — right at the end of the big building boom. Two blocks east, Henry Doelger's model homes got patriotic names as the war neared: his Rainbow House on 42nd (1941) and Freedom House on 43rd (1942), among the last before wartime rules halted building ([Western Neighborhoods Project](https://www.outsidelands.org/doelger-types.php), [SF Planning](https://default.sfplanning.org/Preservation/sunset_survey/Adopted_SunsetHCS.pdf)).
- About a five-minute walk southwest, the Noriega seawall dates from the 1980s, and wind still piles sand over it every year — Public Works moved 30,000 cubic yards there in June 2023, timed for after the plovers leave ([Public Works](https://sfpublicworks.org/node/2398)).
- Half a mile down the beach, the 1878 clipper King Philip still lies buried under the sand near Noriega and Ortega; her ribs surface after big winter storms ([NPS](https://home.nps.gov/goga/learn/historyculture/vestiges-shipwrecks.htm)).

The archive also has two old photographs pinned right near 46th and Moraga ([wnp58.929](https://opensfhistory.org/Display/wnp58.929.jpg), [wnp58.923](https://opensfhistory.org/Display/wnp58.923.jpg)).

And like every block out here, you're standing on dune sand, with the San Andreas Fault running 2–3 miles offshore.

If you know something about the block — who built your house, what stood at the corner — I'd be glad to add it to the notes for the next person.
